question.prompt:
The magnitudes of the sides of triangle \(ABC\) are \(a,\) \(b,\) \(c,\) as shown, with \(c\leq b\leq a.\) Through interior point \(P\) and the vertices \(A,\) \(B,\) \(C,\) lines are drawn meeting the opposite sides in \(A',\) \(B',\) \(C',\) respectively. Let \(s=AA'+BB'+CC'.\) Then, for all positions of point \(P,\) \(s\) is less than:

[Figure 1](figures/1964_AMC_12_Q39_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The figure labels \(BC=a\), \(CA=b\), and \(AB=c\), with \(c\le b\le a\). Because \(P\) is interior, each of \(A',B',C'\) lies strictly between the endpoints of its side. We can bound the three lengths separately.

First consider any nondegenerate triangle \(XYZ\), with \(D\) strictly between \(Y\) and \(Z\). Drop the perpendicular from \(X\) to line \(YZ\), with foot \(H\). On this line,
\[
HD<\max\{HY,HZ\}.
\]
Indeed, if \(H\) is outside the segment, distances increase toward the farther endpoint. If \(H\) is on the segment, \(D\) lies between \(H\) and an endpoint, or equals \(H\), and the same strict bound follows.

For any point \(U\) on line \(YZ\), Pythagoras gives \(XU^2=XH^2+HU^2\); when \(U=H\), this is simply an identity. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
XD^2&=XH^2+HD^2\\
&<XH^2+\max\{HY^2,HZ^2\}\\
&=\max\{XY^2,XZ^2\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Comparing positive lengths yields \(XD<\max\{XY,XZ\}\). This argument also covers triangles whose altitude foot lies outside the opposite side.

Apply the bound at the three vertices:
\[
\begin{aligned}
AA'&<\max\{AB,AC\}=b,\\
BB'&<\max\{BA,BC\}=a,\\
CC'&<\max\{CA,CB\}=a.
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding gives \(\boxed{s<2a+b}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\). The inequalities remain strict even when some side lengths are equal, because the side intersections are interior.
solutions.title: Compare distances using an altitude

solutions.explanation:
A parallel construction lets us compare each cevian with a broken path whose length is a weighted average of the two adjacent sides.

In a nondegenerate triangle \(XYZ\), let \(D\) lie strictly between \(Y\) and \(Z\), and put
\[
t=\frac{YD}{YZ},\qquad 0<t<1.
\]
Through \(D\), draw the parallel to \(XY\), meeting \(XZ\) at \(E\). The proportional-segment theorem gives
\[
ZE=(1-t)XZ,\qquad ED=(1-t)XY.
\]
Thus \(XE=tXZ\). The triangle inequality in triangle \(XED\) now gives
\[
XD<XE+ED=tXZ+(1-t)XY.
\]
Both coefficients are positive and sum to \(1\), so the expression on the right is at most the larger of \(XY\) and \(XZ\). Consequently,
\[
XD<\max\{XY,XZ\}.
\]
In the given figure, \(BC=a\), \(CA=b\), and \(AB=c\). Since \(P\) is interior, all three opposite-side intersections are interior, so this bound applies to each cevian:
\[
AA'<b,\qquad BB'<a,\qquad CC'<a.
\]
These bounds use only \(c\le b\le a\); equal side lengths cause no exception because the triangle inequality above is strict. Adding yields \(\boxed{s<2a+b}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutions.title: Use a parallel and the triangle inequality
